title: No charges laid in RCMP-involved shooting of Brydon Bryce Whitstone
subtitle: There will be no charges laid against the RCMP member who shot and killed Brydon Bryce Whitsone in October 2017.
article: There will be no charges laid against the RCMP member who shot and killed Brydon Bryce Whitsone in October 2017, Saskatchewan's Ministry of Justice says.

Whitstone, 22, from Onion Lake Cree Nation, died after being shot on Oct. 21, 2017. RCMP have said they pursued a vehicle after reports of a man being chased and shot at in North Battleford. The chase ended shortly after the suspect rammed a cruiser. RCMP said previously that an officer fired on the vehicle "in response to the driver's actions."
On Tuesday, Ministry of Justice spokesman Drew Wilby said investigations into the death have concluded and no charges would be laid.

Results of the investigation, which was led by the Regina Police Service, were relayed to public prosecutors, who determined there would be no charges, Wilby said. A coroner's inquest into the death is scheduled to be held in North Battleford from Dec. 3-7, 2018.

Wilby called the death "a terribly unfortunate incident" that resulted in the loss of a father and a friend but that he was unable to provide extensive details into the investigation, as the inquest still needs to take place.

Wilby said the role of the Regina Police Service was to gather facts and evidence without bias to determine if the RCMP member acted in contravention to his authority as a police officer and if the officer was criminally responsible for the Whitstone's death. Wilby said members of the investigation team met with members of Whitstone's family earlier on Tuesday to relay the results.
"I want to assure you that we're confident in the investigation and the process that was followed," said Wilby.
The family of Whitstone says they hope an inquest will tell them why police felt the need to open fire.
"Why did he shoot him twice? Why did he even shoot him?" said Whitstone's mother, Dorothy Laboucane, when asked about the inquest.
Laboucane wonders why officers didn't Taser her son instead of killing him. She said it's about time that an inquest was called.
"My whole family needs closure, we need answers and we need to get to the bottom of this, the truth," she said.

Ron Piche, the lawyer representing Whitstone's family, said there have been many delays in the family's attempt to get information about the shooting. He hopes the inquest will allow the family to get some of their questions answered.
"Whether at the end of the day the answers they receive are going to be accepted or acceptable to them, we'll leave that for the inquest itself," Piche said.
Wilby asked that people refrain from making inflammatory remarks on social media, saying there were a number of lessons learned during the process.
While it was a "terrible incident" that prompted the investigation Wilby said, "I think it shows the process in Saskatchewan was comprehensive, I think it showed that it worked."

RCMP in a statement said that while it has conducted an internal review into the the circumstances leading up to and including Whitstone's death, and is committed to advising the public on its outcome, it is not in a position to release the results due to the pending inquest.
"It is critical that we protect the integrity of the inquest," RCMP said.
RCMP said it welcomed the coroner's inquest, calling it a "fact-finding process that will allow for full disclosure of the facts as they pertain to this case.

"During the inquest, we expect to disclose our members' role in this matter including all investigative/enforcement steps that were taken with the ultimate goal of ensuring public and officer safety during critical incidents such as this."
While the cause of death has not been released, family members told the Saskatoon StarPhoenix that Whitstone died as a result of two gunshot wounds to the chest, based on preliminary autopsy results.
The inquest is scheduled to take place in North Battleford Court of Queen's Bench.
